mainTopic: When the שליח ציבור fulfills others' obligation in תפילה, why ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים are special, and preparing one's prayer.
overview: This amud finishes the discussion of whether the שליח ציבור can fulfill the congregation's obligation in תפילה. רבי יוחנן said both 'מודים חכמים לרבן גמליאל' and 'הלכה כרבן גמליאל', which seem to clash. רבי אבא first splits the topics, but that answer is rejected. רב נחמן בר יצחק then splits the people instead: רבי מאיר agrees with רבן גמליאל for ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, and the רבנן argue, as a ברייתא shows. The גמרא explains that רבי מאיר's reason is that these blessings are long, not that they have many verses, since saying 'וּבְתוֹרָתְךָ כָּתוּב לֵאמֹר' is enough for a יחיד and a צבור alike. רבי אלעזר teaches that a person should prepare his prayer first, and רבי אבא limits this to rare prayers, like those of רב יהודה, who prayed only once every thirty days. Finally, רבין's version teaches that רבן גמליאל let the שליח ציבור exempt only people held back by work in the fields, not city people. The amud closes with the הדרן, completing מסכת ראש השנה.

steps.title: Rabbi Abba splits the topics: holidays versus the whole year
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא settles the clash in רבי יוחנן's words. The חכמים agree with רבן גמליאל on ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, and they still argue about the blessings of the rest of the year.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי אבא came back from the sea, he explained it: the חכמים agree with רבן גמליאל about the blessings of ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים. And the statement 'the הלכה follows רבן גמליאל', which implies they argue, is about the blessings of the whole year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction it raised earlier between רבי יוחנן's two statements. It does this by saying each statement is about a different set of blessings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'הלכה כ...' assumes there is a disagreement, while 'מודים' means there is none. רבי אבא says both are true, but on different topics. On ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים everyone agrees the שליח ציבור fulfills the obligation for everyone, and on regular days of the year there is still an argument.

keyTerms.meaning: When he came up. With מִיַּמֵּי it means when he returned from his sea voyage.
He explained it
The Sages agree (concede)
Which implies that they argue

steps.confusionAlert: 'הלכה כרבן גמליאל' is not just a ruling here. The גמרא treats the word 'הלכה' itself as a clue that there must be a disagreement, because nobody says 'the הלכה follows X' when everyone already agrees.

phrases.english: When Rabbi Abba came back from the sea,
he explained it:
The Sages agree with Rabban Gamliel

phrases.aramaic: בִּבְרָכוֹת שֶׁל רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה וְשֶׁל יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים,
phrases.english: regarding the blessings of Rosh HaShana and of Yom Kippur,
and 'the halacha follows him', which implies they disagree,
phrases.notes: Refers to רבי יוחנן's other statement.

phrases.english: is about the blessings of the whole year.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי סְלֵיק רַבִּי אַבָּא מִיַּמֵּי, פֵּירְשַׁהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction between רבי יוחנן's two statements, which was raised on the previous amud.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the topics: different sets of blessings
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both of רבי יוחנן's statements seem to address the same blessings, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'מודים' is about ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, and 'הלכה' is about the blessings of the rest of the year.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן said 'הלכה' about the holidays themselves
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks רבי אבא's answer. רבי חנה ציפוראה quotes רבי יוחנן saying 'הלכה כרבן גמליאל' specifically about ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבי חנה ציפוראה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: the הלכה follows רבן גמליאל in the blessings of ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אבא's answer. It quotes a version of רבי יוחנן's statement that uses the word 'הלכה' about the very holidays where רבי אבא said everyone agrees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא claimed that on ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים there is no argument. But 'הלכה' implies an argument, and here רבי יוחנן uses it exactly about those days. So there must be someone who argues even on ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, and רבי אבא's way of splitting the topics fails.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? (introduces a challenge)
But didn't he say...?
From the city of ציפורי

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But didn't Rabbi Chana of Tzippori say
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
The halacha follows Rabban Gamliel

phrases.aramaic: בִּבְרָכוֹת שֶׁל רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה וְשֶׁל יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים!
phrases.english: in the blessings of Rosh HaShana and of Yom Kippur!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי חָנָה צִיפּוֹרָאָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אבא's answer in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבא's claim that there is full agreement on ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן used the word 'הלכה', which implies an argument, about ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים themselves. So the argument cannot be limited to the rest of the year.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק splits the people instead of the topics
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says both statements are about ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, but they refer to different תנאים. רבי מאיר is the one who agrees with רבן גמליאל, and the רבנן are the ones who argue.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Who are the ones who 'agree'? רבי מאיר. And the statement 'the הלכה follows him', which implies they argue, refers to the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer to replace רבי אבא's rejected one. This time the split is about who is agreeing and who is arguing, not about which days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אלא' signals that the first answer is dropped. Both of רבי יוחנן's statements now address ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים. 'מודים' means one תנא, רבי מאיר, agrees with רבן גמליאל on those days, while 'הלכה' means other תנאים, the רבנן, still argue, and the הלכה follows רבן גמליאל against them.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops the earlier answer and gives a new one)
Who?
The Rabbis (the majority of Sages)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'חכמים' in 'מודים חכמים' turns out to mean רבי מאיר, not the regular group of חכמים who argue with רבן גמליאל in the משנה.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
Who are the ones who agree? Rabbi Meir,
and 'the halacha', which implies they disagree, refers to the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: מַאן מוֹדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רבי אבא's answer, which step 2 knocked down.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both statements describe the same group, so 'agree' and 'argue' contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר agrees with רבן גמליאל on ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, the רבנן argue, and the הלכה follows רבן גמליאל.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows רבי מאיר agrees and the רבנן argue
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports רב נחמן בר יצחק. רבי מאיר says the שליח ציבור fulfills the obligation for everyone in the ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים blessings, while the חכמים require every individual to say them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: in the blessings of ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, the שליח ציבור fulfills the obligation for the many. These are the words of רבי מאיר. And the חכמים say: just as the שליח ציבור is obligated, so too every single individual is obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רב נחמן בר יצחק's answer. It shows a real disagreement about ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, with רבי מאיר on רבן גמליאל's side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר limits his ruling to ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים. So he agrees with רבן גמליאל only on those days, which is what 'מודים' refers to. The חכמים disagree even on those days, which is why רבי יוחנן needed to say 'הלכה כרבן גמליאל'.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
The prayer leader
Fulfills their obligation for them
An individual

steps.whatToRemember: Final picture: רבי מאיר agrees with רבן גמליאל only for ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, and the חכמים disagree even there. רבי יוחנן rules like רבן גמליאל for those days.
steps.whyThisMatters: The blessings of ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים are long and unfamiliar. This is why the שליח ציבור can fulfill the obligation for people who cannot say them on their own.

phrases.english: As it was taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: בְּרָכוֹת שֶׁל רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה וְשֶׁל יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים —
phrases.english: The blessings of Rosh HaShana and of Yom Kippur:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלִיחַ צִבּוּר מוֹצִיא הָרַבִּים יְדֵי חוֹבָתָן,
phrases.english: the prayer leader fulfills the obligation for the many,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Sages say:
Just as the prayer leader is obligated,
so too every single individual is obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves רב נחמן בר יצחק's answer from step 3.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן בר יצחק's claim that רבי מאיר agrees with רבן גמליאל and the רבנן disagree
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא recording the argument between רבי מאיר and the חכמים about the ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים blessings

steps.title: What makes these blessings different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי מאיר agrees with רבן גמליאל only for the blessings of ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about these blessings?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question about the ברייתא from Step 4. Why does רבי מאיר let the שליח ציבור fulfill everyone's obligation only on ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים, and not during the rest of the year?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 showed that רבי מאיר makes a distinction between these days and the rest of the year. The גמרא now wants the reason behind that distinction. This question opens the next discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? The גמרא asks for the reason behind a distinction.
These, meaning the blessings of ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים

phrases.english: What is different about these (blessings)?
phrases.notes: 'These' means the ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים blessings, where רבי מאיר agrees with רבן גמליאל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind רבי מאיר's distinction in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים blessings are treated differently from the blessings of the rest of the year.

steps.title: First suggestion: these blessings have many verses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the reason is the many פסוקים included in these blessings.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is because they have many verses...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a first possible answer: these blessings contain many verses, which makes them hard for an individual to say. The next step will knock this answer down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ראש השנה מוסף has מלכיות, זכרונות, and שופרות, and each one includes many פסוקים. The idea is that people may not know all these verses, so the שליח ציבור says them for everyone. The word אִילֵּימָא tells us this is only a trial answer.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say. This word introduces a trial answer that will soon be rejected.
There are many verses

steps.confusionAlert: אִילֵּימָא means this is NOT the final answer. Do not take it as the conclusion.

phrases.english: If you say it is because the verses are many —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a trial answer to the question in Step 5.

steps.title: Rejected: you do not have to say the verses
steps.stepSummary: רב's rule shows that saying 'וּבְתוֹרָתְךָ כָּתוּב לֵאמֹר' is enough, so the number of verses cannot be the reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רב חננאל say in the name of רב: Once a person has said 'And in Your Torah it is written, saying,' he no longer needs (to say the verses)!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the first suggestion. According to רב, a person does not have to say the verses at all, so having many verses cannot make these blessings hard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the opening line 'וּבְתוֹרָתְךָ כָּתוּב לֵאמֹר' is enough on its own, the verses are optional. Optional verses cannot explain why a person would need the שליח ציבור. So the reason must be something else.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? This introduces a source that contradicts what was just said.
'And in Your Torah it is written, saying.' This line introduces the verses in the blessing.
He no longer needs to (say the verses)

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Chananel say in the name of Rav:
Once he has said, 'And in Your Torah it is written, saying,'
he no longer needs (to recite the verses)!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the trial answer of Step 6.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggestion that the many verses are the reason for the distinction
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: According to רב, the verses do not have to be said at all, so they cannot be what makes the blessings difficult.

steps.title: The real reason: the blessings are long
steps.stepSummary: The real reason is that there are many long blessings, which are hard to know by heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is because the blessings are many.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its real answer. The ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים blessings are many and long, so many people cannot say them properly on their own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is not the verses. The problem is the text of the blessings themselves, which is long and is said only once a year. That is why רבי מאיר lets the שליח ציבור fulfill the obligation for everyone on these days.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. This introduces the corrected answer.
The blessings are many and long

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר lets the שליח ציבור fulfill everyone's obligation on ראש השנה and יום הכיפורים because the blessings are long and unfamiliar, not because of the verses.

phrases.english: Rather, it is because the blessings are many (and long).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer with the correct one.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The blessings themselves are numerous and long.

steps.title: Looking at רב's rule on its own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings back רב's statement in order to discuss it directly.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter itself: רב חננאל said in the name of רב: Once a person has said 'And in Your Torah it is written, saying,' he no longer needs (to say the verses).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats רב's rule, this time to study it for its own sake. This sets up the next steps, which ask how far the rule goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word גּוּפָא signals that a statement quoted earlier only in passing will now be examined directly. The rule is that the opening line is enough even without saying the verses.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter itself. The גמרא returns to examine a statement it quoted earlier.

phrases.aramaic: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַב חֲנַנְאֵל אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: The matter itself: Rav Chananel said in the name of Rav:
Once he has said, 'And in Your Torah it is written, saying,' —
he no longer needs (to recite the verses).

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַב חֲנַנְאֵל אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the source used in Step 7 and examines it directly.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Saying 'וּבְתוֹרָתְךָ כָּתוּב לֵאמֹר' is enough without saying the verses.

steps.title: Some thought the rule was only for an individual
steps.stepSummary: Some understood that רב's rule applies only to a יחיד and not to a צבור.
steps.simpleTranslation: They understood from this: This applies only to an individual, but for a congregation, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports how some people first understood רב's rule. They limited it to someone praying alone, and the next step will correct this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea was that a public prayer needs to be complete, so the verses would have to be said there. This is a הוה אמינא, a first impression, which will be overturned.

keyTerms.meaning: They understood from it. This introduces a first impression that is later corrected.
An individual praying alone
A congregation

phrases.english: They understood from this:
this applies only to an individual,
but for a congregation, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a limited reading of רב's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First impression: the rule applies only to a יחיד.

steps.title: The rule applies to individual and congregation alike
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי says the rule applies equally to a יחיד and a צבור.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: Whether an individual or a congregation, once he has said 'And in Your Torah it is written, saying,' he no longer needs (to say the verses).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the narrow reading by quoting רבי יהושע בן לוי. He says the rule is the same for a יחיד and for a צבור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The limit suggested in Step 10 is removed. Even the שליח ציבור praying for the צבור does not have to say the verses after the opening line.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated. This introduces a statement of an אמורא.
Both an individual and a congregation

steps.whatToRemember: Saying 'וּבְתוֹרָתְךָ כָּתוּב לֵאמֹר' is enough, both for a יחיד and for a צבור.

phrases.aramaic: אִתְּמַר, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי:
phrases.english: It was stated: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Whether an individual or a congregation,
once he has said, 'And in Your Torah it is written, saying,' —
he no longer needs (to recite the verses).

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Overturns the limited reading of Step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that רב's rule applies only to a יחיד
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי יהושע בן לוי explicitly includes the צבור.

steps.title: Arrange your prayer before praying
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר teaches that a person should first arrange his תפילה and only then pray.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: A person should always arrange his prayer, and afterwards pray.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from רבי אלעזר: get your prayer in order before you start praying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opens a new topic, connected to the theme of hard and unfamiliar blessings. Arranging the prayer means preparing it so that you can say it smoothly and correctly.

keyTerms.meaning: Always
Should arrange or prepare (his prayer)

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
A person should always arrange his prayer,
and afterwards pray.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: לְעוֹלָם יַסְדִּיר אָדָם תְּפִלָּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, related topic about preparing to pray.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should prepare his prayer before praying.

steps.title: This applies only to rare prayers
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא limits רבי אלעזר's rule to ראש השנה, יום הכיפורים, and occasional prayers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said: רבי אלעזר's statement makes sense for the blessings of ראש השנה, יום הכיפורים, and occasional prayers, but not for the prayers of the whole year.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא explains how far רבי אלעזר's rule reaches. He says you need to prepare only for prayers that you do not say often.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Daily prayers are already familiar, so there is no need to arrange them first. Rare prayers, such as those of ראש השנה, יום הכיפורים, and the festivals, need preparation.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense
Occasional times, such as festivals or prayers said only from time to time

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said:
Rabbi Elazar's statement is reasonable
for the blessings of Rosh Hashanah
and of Yom Kippur and of occasional times,
but for (the prayers of) the whole year — no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows רבי אלעזר's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Preparing the prayer is needed only for rare prayers.

steps.title: But רב יהודה prepared even ordinary prayers
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה prepared his prayer before praying, which seems to go against רבי אבא's limit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רב יהודה would arrange his prayer and then pray!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אבא. רב יהודה prepared his prayer even on regular days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If preparation is needed only for rare prayers, why did רב יהודה prepare his ordinary weekday prayers? His practice seems to support preparing all the time.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? This introduces a challenge.
Arranged his prayer

phrases.english: Is that so?!

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא רַב יְהוּדָה מְסַדַּר צְלוֹתֵיהּ וּמְצַלֵּי!
phrases.english: But Rav Yehuda would arrange his prayer and then pray!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָא רַב יְהוּדָה מְסַדַּר צְלוֹתֵיהּ וּמְצַלֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי אבא's limit.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבא's claim that everyday prayers do not need preparation
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב יהודה prepared even his everyday prayers.

steps.title: רב יהודה prayed only every thirty days
steps.stepSummary: Because רב יהודה prayed only once every thirty days, even his regular prayers counted as occasional ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה is different. Since he prayed only every thirty days, his prayers were like occasional prayers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. For רב יהודה, ordinary prayers were rare, so they needed preparation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה was busy learning תורה and prayed only once a month. For him, the daily prayers were unfamiliar, just like festival prayers. So רבי אבא's rule still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different. This introduces a distinction.
It is similar to

steps.whatToRemember: Preparing one's prayer is needed for prayers that are unfamiliar, and how familiar a prayer is depends on how often the person says it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the rule depends on how familiar the prayer is to the person, not on the calendar alone.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda is different,
since from thirty days to thirty days
he would pray,
(his prayers) are like occasional prayers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יהודה prepared even ordinary prayers, which would mean all prayers need preparation.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רב יהודה, the prayers were rare, so they counted like occasional prayers.

steps.title: רבן גמליאל exempted even people in the fields
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר עוירא, quoting רבי שמעון חסידא, reports that רבן גמליאל let the שליח צבור exempt even people working in the fields.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר עוירא said in the name of רבי שמעון חסידא: רבן גמליאל would exempt even the people in the fields.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement about how wide רבן גמליאל's rule is: the שליח צבור's prayer counts even for people who were not in שול at all, but out in the fields.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל holds that the שליח צבור can fulfill the prayer obligation for others. This statement says his rule reaches people far away who never came to שול. The word 'אפילו' (even) suggests that this is the farthest case, so closer people would surely be included too.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempts, meaning the שליח צבור's prayer fulfills their obligation
The תנא who holds that the שליח צבור fulfills the obligation for others
People who are out in the fields, working away from the town
Even. It signals that this is the most extreme case

phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Avira said
Rabbi Shimon Chasida said:
Rabban Gamliel would exempt
even the people who are in the fields.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר עַוִּירָא אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן חֲסִידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the topic of preparing one's prayer to the scope of רבן גמליאל's rule about the שליח צבור exempting others.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to this report, רבן גמליאל's exemption reaches even people out in the fields.

steps.title: So surely people in the city are included
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws the obvious inference: if even field workers are exempted, then city people who did not come to שול are certainly exempted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it goes without saying that those who are here in the city are exempted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from the word 'even' in the last statement. It is setting up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reasoning is: field workers are far away, and city people are close by. If the far ones are covered, the close ones should surely be covered too. The next step will attack this assumption.

keyTerms.meaning: And it goes without saying; and certainly
Who are standing here, meaning in the city

phrases.english: And it goes without saying
those who are here (in the city)?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an implication from the word 'אפילו' in step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the statement means that city people who did not come to שול are, all the more so, exempted.

steps.title: On the contrary: field workers have an excuse, city people do not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the inference. Field workers are held back by their work, so they deserve the exemption. City people have no such excuse.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! These (in the fields) are held back by circumstances beyond their control, but those (in the city) are not held back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא flips the logic around. The field workers are actually the EASIER case for an exemption, not the harder one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deciding factor is not distance. It is whether the person had a real excuse for missing. A city person could have come to שול and chose not to, so it makes sense that he should not be exempted. This challenges the 'surely the city people' inference, and with it the 'אפילו' version of the statement.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary; the opposite makes more sense
They are held back by circumstances beyond their control (אונס)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think 'far away = harder case.' Here the key question is whether the person had an excuse (אונס), not how far away he was. That is why the field workers come out BETTER than the city people.

phrases.english: On the contrary:
these (in the fields) are held back by circumstances beyond their control,
those (in the city) are not held back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inference made in step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that city people are certainly exempted, and so the 'אפילו' version of רבי שמעון חסידא's statement.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An exemption makes sense for someone held back by אונס, not for someone who could have come and did not.

steps.title: Support from the ברייתא about people behind the כהנים
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that people standing behind the כהנים are not included in ברכת כהנים. This shows that someone who could have made the effort and did not loses out.
steps.simpleTranslation: As אבא, son of רב בנימין בר חייא, taught: People who are behind the כהנים are not included in the blessing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up the 'on the contrary' argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People standing behind the כהנים could easily have moved to the front, so they are left out of the ברכה. People in the fields, who cannot come, are included. In the same way, city people who could have come to שול are not covered by the שליח צבור, but field workers are.

keyTerms.meaning: As was taught (in a ברייתא)
Behind the כהנים, not facing them during ברכת כהנים
Included in the blessing

phrases.aramaic: דְּתָנֵי אַבָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב בִּנְיָמִין בַּר חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: As Abba, son of Rav Binyamin bar Chiya, taught:
People who are behind the priests
are not included in the blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתָנֵי אַבָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב בִּנְיָמִין בַּר חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the 'אדרבה' argument of step 18.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that someone who could have taken part and did not is excluded, while someone held back by אונס is included.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of אבא בריה דרב בנימין בר חייא about people standing behind the כהנים.

steps.title: Corrected version: רבן גמליאל exempted only the field workers
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports a different version of רבי שמעון חסידא's statement: רבן גמליאל exempted ONLY the people in the fields, because they are held back by work. People in the city are not exempted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רבין came, he said that רבי יעקב בר אידי said in the name of רבי שמעון חסידא: רבן גמליאל exempted only the people in the fields. What is the reason? Because they are held back by their work. But those in the city, no.
steps.whatsHappening: Because of the challenge, the גמרא drops the first version and brings רבין's corrected report of the same teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אפילו' (even) is replaced by 'only' (לא… אלא). The reason is spelled out: the field workers are held back by their work. City people could come to שול, so they must pray for themselves.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It signals that the earlier version is being replaced
When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
What is the reason?
Work, here field labor

steps.whatToRemember: According to the final version, רבן גמליאל's exemption by the שליח צבור applies only to people held back by אונס, such as field workers. People in the city who simply did not come must pray on their own.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רבן גמליאל's rule is not an automatic exemption for everyone. It is built around אונס, which is why the city/field distinction matters.

phrases.english: Rather, when Ravin came:
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi said
that Rabbi Shimon Chasida said:
Rabban Gamliel exempted no one
except the people in the fields.
What is the reason?
Because they are held back by their work.
But those in the city, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the version of step 16 in answer to the challenge of steps 18 and 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Corrected version of the tradition: 'only' instead of 'even'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבן גמליאל exempted even field workers, and all the more so city people.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבן גמליאל exempted only field workers, who are held back by their work. City people are not exempted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The שליח צבור exempts only people held back by אונס, such as field workers, and not people in the city.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing פרק יום טוב and completing מסכת ראש השנה
steps.stepSummary: The traditional הדרן line closes the fourth פרק, יום טוב, and announces that מסכת ראש השנה is finished.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, פרק יום טוב, and מסכת ראש השנה is now complete.
steps.whatsHappening: This is not a new argument. It is the closing line that marks the end of the פרק and the end of the whole מסכת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words הדרן עלך mean "we will return to you." They express the learner's commitment not to say goodbye forever, but to come back and review. The extra phrase וסליקא לה tells us this was the last פרק of the מסכת, so the whole tractate is now complete.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you. The traditional formula said when finishing a פרק.
The name of this fourth פרק, taken from its opening words: יום טוב של ראש השנה.
And it is completed. Used when the last פרק of a מסכת is finished.
The tractate dealing with ראש השנה, קידוש החודש, and תקיעת שופר.

steps.whatToRemember: The מסכת ends with רבן גמליאל's ruling as reported by רבין: the שליח צבור exempts only people held back by their work in the fields, not city people who simply chose not to come to שול.
steps.whyThisMatters: Finishing a מסכת is a סיום. The custom is to say the הדרן and to commit to returning to the learning, showing that Torah study is never truly "done."

phrases.english: We will return to you, [chapter] Yom Tov
phrases.notes: The standard closing formula for a chapter. The chapter is named for its opening words.

phrases.english: and Tractate Rosh Hashanah is completed
phrases.notes: Added only when the final chapter of a tractate is finished.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַדְרָן עֲלָךְ יוֹם טוֹב וּסְלִיקָא לַהּ מַסֶּכֶת רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Formally closes the sugya that ended in step 20 with רבין's version of רבן גמליאל's ruling. It also closes the entire פרק and מסכת.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: פרק יום טוב and מסכת ראש השנה are complete. The final halachic point is that the שליח צבור exempts only those held back by work (people in the fields), not city people who could have come.
